games.explanation: Detmers has a strikeout rate that hides how much damage right-handed bats do when they actually put the ball in play against him, and Baltimore just happens to run out a lineup full of righties who hit the ball loud. Alonso and Henderson are the exact profile that turns his flyball tendencies into a problem at this park, and the barrel rate he's coughed up to righties this year is genuinely alarming. Trevor Rogers, meanwhile, has quietly been one of the more efficient arms nobody talks about, sporting a wOBA-against under .240 that the market keeps refusing to price in. Halos rank as clear underdogs by Elo and their lineup gets thin fast after Neto and Trout. -118 on the better team, the better arm, and the better matchup is the kind of chalk worth writing down.

Jacob Lopez has quietly been the kind of walk-prone lefty who gets exposed when the lineup he faces is deeper than his, and Cincinnati happens to be that lineup by a wide margin tonight. Right-handed bats have tagged him for a .307 xwOBA with an 11% walk rate, which is exactly the profile Elly, Stewart, and Steer are built to punish in a park that turns fly balls into souvenirs. The Athletics counter with a lineup that leans on Soderstrom and Langeliers to do all the damage, and neither one erases a 184-point Elo gap by himself. -134 is a fair number on the better team in a bandbox against a pitcher who gives the barrels away.

Sean Burke walks the ballpark and gives up loud contact to right-handed hitters, which is a problem when the other dugout has Sonny Gray and a lineup built to punish exactly that profile. Burke is issuing free passes to righties at a double-digit clip while surrendering barrels on nearly one in eight batted balls, and Boston runs Abreu and Contreras straight at him. Gray, meanwhile, is the far steadier arm in this game, with a strikeout-to-walk profile Burke cannot touch. The White Sox are a bad team being asked to out-slug a better one on the road, and -125 is a small price for the right side of that fight.

Getting a plus price on the better team is the kind of gift the market hands out when it's still charging Padres tax on name recognition alone. Casey Mize's contact profile is a problem against this lineup specifically, because Arizona runs Carroll, Marte, and Perdomo out first and Mize has been getting barreled up by righties all year at a 10.3% clip. The roof is closed, the park won't inflate anything, and this projects as a coin-flip game where one team is priced like an underdog and the other isn't. At +110 on the side the simulation prefers, you're getting paid to take the team that should be favored.

The market is pricing this like Bryan Woo is untouchable and Detroit is a coin flip's worst side, when in reality the Tigers are the better team on paper and Woo's shine is thinner than the ERA suggests. Woo runs a barrel rate north of 9% and gives up hard contact on better than 42% of batted balls, which is not the profile of a guy you lay chalk with against a lineup that swings the bat. Riley Greene and Gleyber Torres are the kind of hitters who make command-forward righties sweat, and the roof-closed environment in a pitcher's park keeps the game where Detroit wants it, close. Getting the superior Elo side at plus money is the whole ballgame, and +135 is doing the pitch a favor.

picks.explanation: Houston is the better team and Hunter Brown is the better pitcher, but this line is priced like the Astros are going to run Toronto out of the building, and that's just not how these games tend to go. Brown is genuinely tough on righties, which matters less when Guerrero and Springer are the two bats you actually have to navigate, both carrying xwOBAs north of .375 against right-handed pitching. Taillon isn't an ace but he throws enough strikes to keep a roof game in the 4-4 neighborhood our sim keeps spitting out. Getting a run and a half with a lineup that can hurt you on one swing is the pitch, and -130 is a fair toll for it.
